strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated and timely problem: building an autoregressive video generator that retains a standard LLM architecture (no external text encoder, no architectural divergence), which is valuable for unified multimodal modeling efforts.

MM-RoPE is a technically sound and well-motivated contribution. The paper carefully diagnoses a real limitation of naive 3D RoPE (imbalanced frequency allocation between temporal and spatial channels, aliasing at low-indexed channels) with clear visualizations (Fig. 3b,c) and proposes a principled fix (distributed meta-groups + scaled positions) that is validated via ablations (Fig. 7b, Fig. 9).

AR-DF is a sensible solution to a clearly identified problem (frame-wise loss imbalance from spatial redundancy under diffusion forcing), and the training/inference procedures are described in good algorithmic detail (Algorithms 1-3), with an ablation demonstrating the loss-imbalance issue is mitigated (Fig. 7a) and that the inference-time masking is necessary (Fig. 8).

Extensive ablation studies are provided: number of meta MM-RoPE groups, scaling factor choices, CFG scale sensitivity, inference-time mask ratio, aspect ratio robustness, and inference overhead of different RoPE schemes -- giving good insight into design choices.

The engineering contribution (training with only 48 GPUs, memory-efficient techniques such as chunked cross-entropy, elimination of unneeded language logits) is a practically useful contribution to the community even if the underlying architecture is standard.

Results are competitive across three tasks (T2I, I2V, T2V) against reasonably chosen strong baselines (EMU3, COSMOS-Video2World, OpenSoraPlan), and qualitative comparisons (Fig. 6, C1) support the claims of favorable prompt alignment and fine-grained motion.
The paper is transparent about limitations (data scale, generalization) and includes societal impact discussion.
weaknesses: Core empirical validation of the two main contributions (MM-RoPE, AR-DF) relies almost exclusively on validation/C-loss curves from a small 0.5B ablation model rather than downstream generation-quality metrics (FID, GenEval, VBench) with proper baselines at the model scale actually used for the main results; it would strengthen claims to show MM-RoPE vs M-RoPE and AR-DF vs alternatives directly on GenEval/VBench for the 1.5B/3.6B models.

No formal quantitative ablation table isolating the contribution of AR-DF against alternative masking baselines (e.g., full diffusion forcing, random masking) using end metrics like VBench numbers -- the evidence is largely qualitative/visual (Fig. 8b) and loss-curve-based.

The claimed performance parity with EMU3/COSMOS/OpenSoraPlan is somewhat mixed: on GenEval, Lumos-1 3.6B modestly outperforms EMU3 8B but with far less data/parameters (reasonable); on VBench-T2V, Lumos-1 3.6B (78.32) is noticeably below OpenSoraPlan (77.23 is actually close, but EMU3 80.96 is clearly higher) and below several diffusion baselines, so "comparable" framing is somewhat generous and could be tempered.

Missing explicit comparisons/ablations against other recently proposed video RoPE schemes (VideoRoPE, TAD-RoPE) mentioned in related work -- the paper only compares against vanilla 3D RoPE/M-RoPE, not the most relevant recent alternatives, weakening the novelty positioning claim.

The scaling factor for 3D positions (4,8,8) is chosen empirically without deeper justification/theory, and the paper itself acknowledges this may not be optimal, leaving an important design choice under-motivated.

Reproducibility could be limited: although code/models are promised, exact training data curation (recaptioning pipeline, filtering criteria) and some hyperparameters are only partially specified, and dataset sizes are quite small/non-standard which may hinder direct comparison/reproduction by others.

AR-DF's inference procedure requires manually tuning ρ_inf, and the sensitivity analysis (Fig 8a) shows a fairly narrow acceptable range (0.3-0.7), suggesting the method may not be very robust across different content or resolutions -- this generalizability is not stress-tested beyond the given examples.

The paper's presentation of some figures (e.g. Fig. 2, 5) appears to contain leftover placeholder text/labels (e.g., "V3", "V4", Chinese text fragments visible in extracted content), suggesting incomplete polishing before submission.

strengths: Addresses a practical and relevant problem: building an autoregressive video generator that closely follows standard LLM architecture, avoiding external text encoders and the inefficiency of pure next-token decoding.
Reasonably extensive set of ablations (RoPE schemes, number of meta MM-RoPE groups, scaling factors, inference mask ratio, CFG scale, aspect ratio robustness) that attempt to justify design choices.

Demonstrates that a relatively small-scale, modestly-resourced training run (48 GPUs, 60M images / 10M videos) can achieve performance in the same ballpark as much larger/better-resourced models (e.g., COSMOS-Video2World with 100M videos and 10,000 H100s), which is a useful practical contribution if verified.
Provides qualitative comparisons across T2I, I2V and T2V tasks with visibly competitive sample quality versus some baselines.
Includes a fairly detailed appendix with architecture/training details, a fully worked-out inference algorithm, and discussion of limitations and safeguards.
weaknesses: Quantitative results are, at best, only roughly on par with or sometimes below prior work (e.g., VBench-T2V 78.32 vs EMU3's 80.96; GenEval overall only marginally above EMU3), undermining the strength of the central performance claims; the paper frames these mixed results optimistically ('comparable to') rather than critically.

The core ablations for the proposed MM-RoPE (distributed channel allocation, scaling factors, number of meta groups) are only evaluated via validation/C-loss curves on a small 0.5B toy model, never validated with actual downstream GenEval/VBench numbers at the scale used for the main results, leaving the claimed benefits for the final reported models unverified.

Technical novelty is incremental: MM-RoPE is essentially a redistribution/interleaving of existing M-RoPE channels plus an empirically tuned scaling factor, and AR-DF combines known ingredients (MaskGIT-style discrete diffusion, diffusion forcing, VideoMAE-style tube masking) without a fundamentally new mechanism.

Multiple figures (e.g., Figure 2, and figures on pages 9 and 13) contain obvious leftover placeholder/draft content in Chinese (e.g., '视频自回归模型 (LlamaVGen)', 'V3（暂定，合并两个图）'), indicating the submission is not properly polished/finalized — a significant presentation/quality-control lapse for a top-tier venue submission.

Comparisons omit several directly relevant recent micro-AR video baselines discussed in the related work (e.g., NOVA, Loong, MAGVIT-family, VideoMAR) in the main quantitative tables, limiting the completeness of the evaluation.

The 'unified model' framing is weakened by the fact that the language modeling loss is explicitly dropped during training for memory reasons, meaning the model's claimed compatibility with language understanding/generation is not actually demonstrated or tested.

No wall-clock/throughput comparison against other AR video baselines (e.g., EMU3, NOVA) is provided beyond an internal RoPE latency micro-benchmark, so the claimed efficiency advantage of the discrete-diffusion inference paradigm is not rigorously substantiated against competitors.

Dataset scale (60M images, 10M videos) and resolution (up to 384p) are modest, and the paper does not test or discuss how design choices (e.g., MM-RoPE scaling factors) would need to adapt at larger scale/resolution, limiting generalizability of conclusions.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: building autoregressive video generators that retain pure LLM architecture (no external text encoder, no fundamental architectural divergence), which is valuable for future unified multimodal models.

MM-RoPE is a well-motivated and carefully diagnosed contribution: the paper empirically identifies the imbalanced frequency spectrum issue in vanilla 3D RoPE (via frequency allocation and rotary-speed visualizations) and proposes a distributed, scaled RoPE scheme that is validated through systematic ablations (number of meta components, scaling factors) showing consistent loss improvements.

AR-DF (temporal tube masking + compatible inference-time masking) is a sensible solution to the identified frame-wise loss imbalance problem caused by spatial redundancy, and the paper provides clear qualitative and quantitative evidence (frame-wise validation loss curves, visual comparisons with/without inference masks) supporting its necessity.

Strong efficiency story: training from scratch on only 48 GPUs with modest data (60M images, 10M videos) while achieving performance comparable to substantially larger/better-resourced models (EMU3, COSMOS-Video2World, OpenSoraPlan), which is a meaningful practical contribution.

Reasonably comprehensive experimental evaluation across three tasks/benchmarks (GenEval for T2I, VBench-I2V, VBench-T2V) with both diffusion and autoregressive baselines, plus several useful auxiliary analyses (CFG sensitivity, aspect-ratio robustness, RoPE inference overhead).

Extensive ablation studies isolating the contribution of individual design choices (distributed channel allocation vs. scaled positions, mask ratio sensitivity, number of meta RoPE groups), which strengthens the credibility of the proposed techniques.
Good reproducibility support via detailed architecture/training tables, sequence formatting details, and a fully specified inference algorithm in the appendix.
weaknesses: The manuscript shows clear signs of insufficient proofreading/polish: leftover Chinese placeholder text and draft annotations (e.g., "视频自回归模型 (LlamaVGen)", "V3（暂定，合并两个图）", "V4（暂定）") appear directly in figures, which raises concerns about the overall care taken in preparing the submission and could indicate other overlooked errors.

Comparisons across tables mix models of very different parameter counts, training data scale, and compute budgets (e.g., Lumos-1 1.5B/3.6B vs. EMU3 8B, or vs. COSMOS-Video2World trained on 10x more video data with far more GPUs); while the efficiency framing is a strength, claims of being "comparable" or "on par" should be interpreted cautiously given these confounds rather than treated as like-for-like comparisons.

No human evaluation is included; all quantitative claims rely on automatic metrics (GenEval, VBench), which are known to have biases and may not fully capture perceptual quality or motion realism differences highlighted qualitatively in the paper.

The scaling factors for 3D positions in MM-RoPE (4,8,8) are chosen empirically via loss curves on a small 0.5B model and generalized to larger models without strong theoretical grounding; the authors themselves acknowledge this may not be optimal, leaving open questions about principled tuning for new data/resolutions.

Video generation is restricted to short clips (25 frames) and relatively low resolutions (e.g., 384p); there is no evaluation of longer-horizon generation stability, error accumulation, or how AR-DF scales with longer temporal contexts.

Some ablations (e.g., MM-RoPE component count, scaling factor sensitivity, AR-DF masking effectiveness) are only conducted on the smallest 0.5B model, and it is not fully verified whether these findings/hyperparameter choices transfer cleanly to the 1B/3B models used for final benchmark comparisons.

The related work review of competing micro-AR video approaches (e.g., NOVA, Loong) is thorough in prose but these methods are not included as direct quantitative baselines in the main results tables, limiting direct empirical positioning against the closest prior work.
